source_read: PMC HTML (PMC10083934; Drug Alcohol Rev 2023;42(1):7-19), saved plain text of the PMC article page read start to end: abstract and key points, Introduction, Methods 2.1-2.8, Results 3.1-3.11 with Table 1 (included studies) and Table 2 (meta-analysis and GRADE summary), Discussion 4.1-4.4, Conclusion, conflict-of-interest statement, supplementary-file list and reference list. Figure 1 (PRISMA flow) and Figure 2 (risk-of-bias graph) are images absent from the text (legends only), so the per-study risk-of-bias judgments could not be read; supplementary files (Figure S2 forest plots, Table S2 GRADE summary of findings, Table S1 extraction template) were not available.

claims.overstatement: Slight: 'Amineptine ... reduced discontinuation' states as a finding what the authors hedge (abstract: amineptine 'may reduce' discontinuation rates); the claim does attach 'very low certainty', so 'may have reduced' would match the source more closely. Nothing else overstated.
claims.note: Reading cautions (not errors): (a) 'no medication other than amineptine differed from placebo on any pooled outcome' is accurate, but the intervals are wide (any medication 0.40-1.23) and the authors say explicitly that the evidence cannot show the medications are ineffective; the claim does not say 'ineffective'. (b) Two of the six medications (ibudilast, varenicline) and one modafinil trial never entered a pooled outcome, so that sentence covers four medications; the magnitude's '6 trials, 186 participants' makes this visible. (c) Single trials outside the pooled outcomes did report differences from placebo (mirtazapine on withdrawal scores in one trial, amantadine on fatigue, varenicline on reaction time, ibudilast on 2 of 12 attention measures), so the restriction to 'pooled outcome' is doing real work. Numbers: every number in the statement and magnitude was found in Table 2 and reproduces exactly: discontinuation any medication RR 0.70 (0.40-1.23), 6 trials, 186 participants; mirtazapine 0.96 (0.48-1.92); modafinil 0.67 (0.22-2.03); amantadine 1.33 (0.34-5.24); amineptine 0.22 (0.07-0.72), very low; withdrawal SMD 0.17 (-0.43 to 0.77), 3 trials, 93; craving SMD 0.34 (-0.77 to 1.45), 2 trials, 48. Nine trials of six medications, six at high risk of bias, search to December 2020, market withdrawal in 1999 for liver toxicity and non-medical use, and one trial reporting adverse events by arm are all in the text. No editors' calculation in this claim. 'About 240 participants' is safe but the source is internally inconsistent: the text gives 242, the Table 1 rows sum to 241, and the arm counts given (129 on medication + 138 on placebo, with 48%/52%) sum to 267, presumably because crossover participants are counted in both arms. Section 3.5 says the discontinuation analysis had 188 people, Table 2 and Section 3.1 say 186 (89 medication, 97 placebo; Table 1 rows for the six trials also sum to 186). 'Two small trials by one group': the two amineptine trials (n = 30 and n = 44, both Thai inpatient settings) list the same three authors (references 51 and 54), so the statement is supported from the reference list, not from an explicit statement by the review. The 1999 market-withdrawal date is stated by the review in its Discussion citing two earlier case reports (1996 and 1998), so it is second-hand and the cited reports cannot themselves document a 1999 event; a primary regulatory source would be a better anchor for that sentence. Which six trials were at high risk of bias is shown only in Figure 2 (an image), so I could not check how many of the six pooled trials were high risk.

anchors.locator: Methods > 2.2 Included studies; 2.3 Search methods; Results > 3.2 Comparisons, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Eligible: RCTs of any medication for methamphetamine withdrawal in people with methamphetamine or amphetamine use disorder or withdrawal diagnosed by DSM or ICD; controls could be placebo, treatment as usual or psychosocial therapy if both arms got the same adjuncts. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL and EMBASE searched to December 2020, plus clinicaltrials.gov to December 2020 and reference lists; no language restriction; PROSPERO CRD42021224850. All nine included trials were placebo-controlled.

anchors.locator: Abstract (Key findings); Results > 3.1 Included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1; 3.2 Comparisons
anchors.extracted: Nine RCTs of six medications (mirtazapine, modafinil, ibudilast, amineptine, varenicline, amantadine), 242 participants by the text (Table 1 rows sum to 241); USA 3, Thailand 3, Australia 2, Iran 1; mean trial size 27; about 88% male. Six trials of four medications meta-analysed: 186 participants, 89 on medication (22 mirtazapine, 9 modafinil, 37 amineptine, 21 amantadine) and 97 on placebo. The ibudilast, varenicline and one modafinil trial (Mahoney 2012) were not pooled because they did not report the review's outcomes. Amineptine trials: Jittiwutikan 1997 (n = 30) and Srisurapanont 1999 (n = 44), both Thai inpatient units, same three authors (references 51, 54).

anchors.locator: Results > 3.3 Risk of bias (Figure 2 is an image)
anchors.extracted: RoB 2 across the nine trials: one low, two some concerns, six high. Most frequent problem selective reporting (6 of 9 trials), then randomisation process (5), deviations from intended intervention (3), missing outcome data (2), outcome measurement (1).

Discontinuation = not remaining enrolled at the primary end point. Any medication RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.40-1.23), 6 trials, 186 participants, I2 18%, p = 0.21, GRADE very low. Amineptine 0.22 (0.07-0.72), 2 trials, 74 participants, I2 58%, p = 0.01, very low. Mirtazapine 0.96 (0.48-1.92), 2 trials, 51, I2 0%, very low. Modafinil 0.67 (0.22-2.03), 1 trial, 19. Amantadine 1.33 (0.34-5.24), 1 trial, 42. Text 3.5 gives the pooled set as 188 people.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Withdrawal symptoms and Craving rows); Results > 3.7 Withdrawal symptoms, 1st-3rd paragraphs; 3.8 Cravings
anchors.extracted: Withdrawal symptoms (AWQ or ACSA): SMD 0.17 (-0.43 to 0.77), 3 trials, 93 participants, I2 49%, p = 0.58, GRADE low; by drug amineptine -0.26 (-0.86 to 0.34), mirtazapine 0.17 (-0.54 to 0.89), modafinil 0.86 (-0.09 to 1.82). Sensitivity analysis with other withdrawal scales also non-significant (data not shown). Craving: SMD 0.34 (-0.77 to 1.45), 2 trials, 48 participants, I2 71%, p = 0.55, very low; amineptine -0.19 (-0.92 to 0.54), modafinil 0.95 (-0.01 to 1.92). Positive values mean higher scores on medication.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Global state rows); Results > 3.6 Global state; Abstract (Key findings); Discussion > 4.1 Efficacy, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Global state (BSI-GSI in one trial, CGI in two): amineptine better than placebo (Table 2 and abstract MD -0.49, -0.80 to -0.17, GRADE low; text SMD -0.70, -1.18 to -0.22, p = 0.004); mirtazapine single trial not different; overall not different (Table 2 -0.24, -0.73 to 0.25; text -0.34, -1.06 to 0.25, p = 0.39; I2 69%). Discussion: no medication differed from placebo on discontinuation, global state, craving or withdrawal intensity, amineptine being the exception (global state and discontinuation).

Amineptine on discontinuation downgraded to very low (serious risk of bias, very serious imprecision); mirtazapine on discontinuation very low (very serious risk of bias and imprecision); amineptine on global state low (serious risk of bias and imprecision). Overall certainty across outcomes low to very low.

Amineptine was never approved in several jurisdictions including the USA and was withdrawn from the market voluntarily by its manufacturer in 1999 after reports of liver toxicity and non-medical use (the review cites a 1996 liver-injury case report and a 1998 dependence case report for this). Authors note it has some immediate dopamine-releasing action, which may explain the positive effect.

Only one trial (amantadine vs placebo) gave the number and type of adverse events by arm: RR 2.47 (0.76-8.03), 35 participants, p = 0.13, very low. Three trials described adverse events in prose only and four gave no safety information (Results account for 8 of the 9 trials; the Discussion says four gave prose descriptions). Safety profiles could not be established.

anchors.locator: Results > 3.7 Withdrawal symptoms, last paragraph; 3.11 Findings from studies not included in the meta-analysis
anchors.extracted: Outside the pooled outcomes, single trials reported differences: the Kongsakon mirtazapine trial (n = 20) reported lower AWQ withdrawal scores than placebo (p = 0.03; medians, so not poolable); amantadine reduced fatigue (p < 0.001); one mirtazapine trial found more night awakenings than placebo (p < 0.05); varenicline gave faster visual reaction time (p = 0.025) but no other cognitive gains; ibudilast improved 2 of 12 attention-test measures. Effect sizes mostly not reported.

Authors: evidence insufficient to show any medication is effective, and equally insufficient to show the studied medications are not effective, given small samples and low-to-very-low quality; further high-quality trials could change the findings.

key_findings.correction: All counts, countries and the mean trial size match Abstract, Results 3.1 and Table 1; the editors' 86% (198 of 230 men) reproduces.

The one-trial domain is described in the source as 'measurement of the intervention' because assessor blinding was unclear, i.e. the outcome-measurement domain; Figure 2 is an image here too, so the trial-by-trial judgments were not readable.
Table 2 values and the Results 3.6 SMD values both reproduce as given.

'Positive values favour placebo' is the card's inference from scale direction (higher score = more symptoms; the QECCRR was sign-reversed for craving); the review does not state the direction for the withdrawal analysis in words. The inference is sound.

Note that Results 3.9 accounts for only 8 of the 9 trials (the 1997 amineptine trial is not mentioned) and Discussion 4.2 says four trials gave prose-only descriptions where Results names three; see 'missed'.

Results 3.1 says the search 'yielded 20 results', 11 of which did not meet the inclusion criteria (references 38-48, two of which, 43 and 47, are e-page conference-abstract citations). The text does not call the 20 'full texts'; that they were full-text assessments is a plausible inference, but the screening counts are only in the PRISMA figure (an image). Suggested wording: 'the search yielded 20 reports, 11 of which did not meet the criteria'. The rest of the finding (four databases to December 2020, ClinicalTrials.gov, reference lists, no language limits) is confirmed at Methods 2.3.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract (Approach) says weighted mean differences; Methods 2.8 says SMD; Table 2 labels global state as mean difference; Results 3.6 gives SMDs with different values. All as stated.

Recomputed: every other Table 2 estimate sits at the midpoint of its interval (relative risks on the log scale, e.g. amineptine sqrt(0.07 x 0.72) = 0.224); mirtazapine global state 0.30 lies outside -0.22 to 0.25; the text's overall SMD -0.34 has interval midpoint -0.405. The text's amineptine (-0.70) and mirtazapine (0.42) SMDs are centred.

242 (text) vs 241 (Table 1 rows) vs 267 (129 + 138, with 48%/52% computed on 267) vs 188 (Results 3.5) vs 186 (Table 2, Results 3.1). The explanation that crossover participants were counted in both arms is the card's inference; the source does not say so, and the arm counts cannot be fully reconciled from the text (the excess of 26 does not map cleanly onto the two crossover trials of 18 and 26).
Recomputed: 16/31 = 51.6% (printed 53%), 20/31 = 64.5% (63%), 12/19 = 63.2% (65%), 18/26 = 69.2% (71%); all other Table 1 percentages match their counts; men 198/230 = 86.1%.

Internal contradiction confirmed: Introduction names amineptine and modafinil; Table 1 dates give amineptine 1997 and 1999 and mirtazapine 2005 and 2008 as the only trials by 2008; the Discussion's 'five additional RCT, two meta-analysed' fits the post-2008 trials (2012, 2013, 2014, 2017, 2018; Lee 2013 and Modarresi 2018 pooled). The consequence's cross-reference is also confirmed from my reading of siefried_2020 (Discussion > Treatment of Withdrawal Symptoms): that review names the 2009 Cochrane review's trials it shares as the 1997 Thai amineptine trial and the 2005 and 2008 mirtazapine trials, plus a fourth trial it did not review.

Article side confirmed (Methods 2.6 lists the five outcomes without calling any primary; Results 3.1 says three trials did not report the 'primary outcomes'; reference 29, cited for Covidence, is a 1995 Australian Institute of Criminology book). The PROSPERO statement (all five outcomes primary) was not checked: the registry record was not available to me in this session.

NOT CHECKED on the registry side rather than absent: the PROSPERO record was not accessible in this session (no web access), so the planned odds ratios, planned time-period and subgroup analyses, English-language limit, database list and comorbidity exclusion could not be checked. Article side confirmed: the article calls the registration prospective (Methods 2.1), reports relative risks (2.8), states no language restriction (2.3), lists MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, EMBASE and ClinicalTrials.gov, reports no time-period or subgroup-by-setting analyses, and acknowledges no deviation from protocol. Treat the registry content of this item as single-reader.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument and the item judgments follow from the article. Items 11 (no investigation of heterogeneity up to I2 71%, inconsistent and partly invalid global-state effect measure) and 15 (publication bias neither assessed nor discussed; GRADE domains listed omit it) are each a critical 'no', so critically low confidence follows from AMSTAR 2's rule (more than one critical flaw). Item 7 'partial yes' fits: the 11 exclusions are cited with only a blanket reason. Item 2 'partial yes' is consistent with the article (prospective registration claimed, no deviation discussed), but its detailed notes rest on the PROSPERO record, which I could not read; if the registry record did not exist before the search started, 'partial yes' would still hold. Agree with the reasoning that the qualitative conclusion is robust to these problems.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right. The three gaps are all present in the text (abstract MD -0.49 vs Results SMD -0.70; Discussion 4.1 moving from two amineptine trials to a research strategy of methamphetamine-like longer-acting drugs; abstract's 'first comprehensive meta-analysis since 2008' framing). One small addition: Results 3.6 describes the continuous global-state effect as amineptine participants being 'more likely to improve', probability wording for a standardized mean difference.

missed: Market-withdrawal sourcing (relevant to cl_meth_withdrawal_medication): the review states the 1999 voluntary withdrawal of amineptine in Discussion 4.1 citing references 64 and 65, a 1996 report of two liver-injury cases and a 1998 report of amineptine and midazolam dependence. Both predate 1999, so the date itself is unreferenced in the review; the claim's 1999 date should be anchored to a primary regulatory or manufacturer source, or worded as 'according to the review'. The same group's 2020 review (siefried_2020, Results > Antidepressants, 1st paragraph) says only that amineptine was never FDA-approved and 'has been suspended in other jurisdictions', with no date or reference, so it does not corroborate 1999.

Safety reporting does not reconcile: Results 3.9 classifies 8 of 9 trials (one with adverse events by arm, three with prose descriptions, four with nothing; the 1997 amineptine trial is not mentioned), while Discussion 4.2 says four trials gave nothing and another four gave prose-only descriptions. Minor; it does not affect the statement that only one trial reported adverse events by arm.
